does_not_prove: A PCM hash covers samples, not speakers: it says nothing about how a device plays them.
The published video carries this narration as 96 kb/s AAC; decoding it does not return these samples.
reproducible means a rebuild on Windows with the same voice and OS build gave the same PCM (checked on the date of this receipt); another machine or voice update need not.

The loudness is one meter's reading (superstack-bs1770/1) of the narration alone, and the peak is the sample peak, not true peak. The narration was normalised to the target with a limiter whose sample-peak ceiling sits 0.5 dB under the true-peak limit; no true-peak meter has read it.
Neither hash shows that the narration is correct, clear, or well paced.

lines: From a proposed answer to a kept receipt.
A local model proposes answers. It is cheap and replaceable, and asking it for more candidates widens the pool.
No learned model sits on this step. An external check, such as a test run or a source comparison, accepts or rejects the answer.
A pass writes a receipt named by a fingerprint of its own contents, so anyone can re-check it offline, and a change to any byte makes that check fail.
When the attempt budget runs out, Flywheel names a stronger tier, a more capable model you can choose to call. It never calls that tier for you.
Passed answers go into a proof cache with their receipts. The next identical request costs nothing, and the cache re-checks the answer before it serves it.
The drawing shows the order of the steps. It does not show that the loop raises accuracy. On the shipped benchmark the interval includes zero.
